meta.descriptionEn: On 28 November 1979 an Air New Zealand DC-10 left Auckland on a one-day sightseeing trip to Antarctica. The crew were experienced, the visibility beneath the cloud base looked clear, and the passengers were holding cameras. Hours later the flight was overdue, and a search began on the most remote continent on Earth. What had gone wrong? Follow the story from the briefing room to the cockpit, from a single changed set of coordinates to a rare whiteout illusion that hid an entire volcano. Then watch two inquiries reach opposite conclusions, a judge face a fierce legal battle, and an airline be forced to face its own record. Discover what aviation learned about navigation data and sector whiteout.
meta.descriptionUr: 28 November 1979 ko Air New Zealand ka ek DC-10 Auckland se Antarctica ki aik din ki sightseeing flight par nikla. Crew tajurbakar tha, mausam saaf lag raha tha aur musafir camere liye baithe the. Chand ghanton baad flight late ho chuki thi aur talash shuru ho gayi. Kya ghalat hua? Is documentary mein dekhein ke kaise coordinates ki aik chhoti si tabdeeli aur whiteout ke dhoke ne sab kuch badal diya, do inquiries ne alag nateeje kyun nikale, aur hawabazi ne navigation data aur sector whiteout se kya seekha.

articleEn: On a cold afternoon over Antarctica, a large passenger jet is flying low. Suddenly a sharp sound fills the cockpit: "Pull up!" It is the ground proximity warning system. First come two whoops, then the machine says clearly: "Pull up!" The flight engineer calls out "500 feet," then "400 feet." With every moment the ground comes closer and time runs out. The captain says, "Go-around power please," meaning full engine power to climb away. But it was too late.

About six seconds later, at 12:50 pm on 28 November 1979, Air New Zealand Flight 901 hit Mount Erebus at an altitude of about 450 metres. There were 237 passengers and 20 crew on board. All of them died in the crash, and we remember them with respect.

The strangest part is that the crew believed they were over McMurdo Sound, many miles from any mountain. So how did nobody see a volcano about 3,800 metres high standing right in front of them? What was changed the night before the crash? And who was finally held responsible: the pilots, the airline, or someone else?
This story involves a small change in a computer, the glare of snow, and two very different inquiries. Let's start from the beginning.

articleEn: In 1977 Air New Zealand began an unusual service: sightseeing flights to Antarctica, where passengers could view the icy continent from the air. The best part was that the whole trip took a single day. The aircraft left in the morning and returned to New Zealand the same day.

On 28 November 1979, Flight 901 left Auckland Airport at 8:00 am. The plan was to spend a few hours over Antarctica and return in the evening. There was a 45-minute stop at Christchurch, where fuel would be loaded and the crew changed. The remaining 747 kilometres would then be flown, arriving in Auckland at 9:00 pm. The distance to Christchurch was about 8,630 kilometres, with arrival planned for 7:00 pm. A ticket cost NZ$359. Every flight also carried an experienced Antarctic guide, who described famous places and views over the PA system.

Sir Edmund Hillary had been a guide on earlier flights. He was supposed to guide on this day too, but declined because of other commitments. His old friend and climbing partner Peter Mulgrew took his place. No one knew this would be the final trip.

Now to the aircraft. For Antarctic flights Air New Zealand had eight McDonnell Douglas DC-10-30 trijets. The one used that day was registered ZK-NZP. It was the 182nd DC-10 built and Air New Zealand's fourth DC-10. It was delivered to the airline at McDonnell Douglas's Long Beach plant on 12 December 1974, and by the time of the crash it had completed more than 20,700 flight hours.

Now to the destination. This is Ross Island, home of Mount Erebus, the southernmost active volcano in the world. McMurdo Station and Scott Base are on the same island, about 35 kilometres away, and scientists study the volcano from there. Erebus is about 3,792 metres high, though one source gives 3,794 metres, a difference of just two metres. Its summit crater holds a lava lake that has existed since at least the early 1970s. The volcano has been active for about 1.3 million years.

Polar explorer Sir James Clark Ross discovered it on 27 January 1841, when it was already erupting. He named it after his ship HMS Erebus, and the neighbouring Mount Terror was named after HMS Terror. In Greek mythology, Erebus is a place of darkness. On this day, a mountain with that name was about to appear in the path of an aircraft.

articleEn: Now let's meet the people in the cockpit. Captain Thomas James, known as Jim Collins, was 45 and regarded as an experienced pilot. He had 11,151 flight hours in total, 2,872 of them on the DC-10, so the aircraft was no stranger to him. First Officer Gregory Mark Cassin was 37, with 7,934 hours overall and 1,361 on the DC-10. Flight Engineer Gordon Brooks was 43, and 3,000 of his 10,886 hours were on the DC-10. The other Flight Engineer, Nick Moloney, was 44, with 6,468 hours in total and 1,700 on the DC-10. First Officer Graham Lucas, aged 39, was also on board.

They were all experienced, but one point matters a great deal. Collins and Cassin had never been to Antarctica before, and Brooks had been only once. Brooks had also served as flight engineer in 1978 on an Air New Zealand flight in the Pacific that involved a rescue for a Cessna 188. Even so, they were considered qualified for this flight.
An important part of the preparation was a briefing held 19 days before the crash. On 9 November 1979 both pilots attended it. They were given a copy of the flight plan from the previous flight.

Here the real confusion begins. The officially approved route, approved in 1977 by New Zealand's Civil Aviation Division, was a different path. That track ran from Cape Hallett straight to the McMurdo NDB, and by coincidence it passed almost directly over the summit of Mount Erebus. But when this route was entered into the computer, a typing error crept into the coordinates. As a result the printout's route changed. It ran south through the middle of McMurdo Sound, about 27 nautical miles, or 50 kilometres, west of Mount Erebus.

Think about it: there were two routes for the same area. One passed through the open Sound, and the other led straight toward a mountain 3,794 metres high. The 9 November briefing showed the Sound plan. So the route explained to the crew differed from the officially approved one.

This was not just one crew's problem. Most of the previous 13 flights had entered the same coordinates into their navigation systems and flown the Sound route. They had no idea the route they were flying did not match the approved one. Everything seemed fine. The night before the flight, Collins marked the route on his map. It was later found that the morning's printout differed from those marks.
So was any mistake caught in the briefing? And what happened before the morning of 28 November that changed everything? That comes in the next part.

articleEn: Let's turn to the night that changed everything. The story starts on 14 November, 14 days before the crash. That day Captain Leslie Simpson, the pilot of another Antarctic flight, noticed something odd. He had also been present at the 9 November briefing. Simpson compared the coordinates of McMurdo's TACAN navigation beacon with the waypoint his crew had entered into the aircraft's inertial navigation system. He was surprised to find a very large gap between the two. The TACAN beacon is about 5 kilometres east of the McMurdo NDB. After his flight, Simpson told Air New Zealand's navigation section about the discrepancy.

This report proved important. It led the navigation section to change the coordinates. The reasons are disputed, but the result was that the ground computer's waypoint was changed. The change was made at about 1:40 am on 28 November, just a few hours before the flight left. The waypoint was changed from 77°53′S 164°48′E to 77°52′S 167°03′E, a longitude difference of more than 2 degrees.

Flight 901's crew was not told about this change. They entered the coordinates from the morning printout into the INS. That printout differed from the flight plan shown at the 9 November briefing, and it did not match the marks on Collins's map either.

The difference was huge. The briefing plan passed through the middle of McMurdo Sound and left Mount Erebus well to the east. But the track on the morning printout passed directly over Mount Erebus. If that stretch had been flown below 4,000 metres, hitting the mountain was certain. Oddly, the original approved route of 1977 also passed roughly over Erebus. Yet the crew had been shown the Sound route in the briefing.

Another change was made in the computer program. The telex sent to the American air traffic controllers at McMurdo Station no longer included the coordinates of the final waypoint. Only the word McMurdo was written instead. So the controllers could not see where the flight's final point had been placed. Later, Justice Mahon concluded that this change was made deliberately, to hide from US authorities that the flight plan had changed. In his view, it was perhaps because it was known that US ATC would object to the new route. That was Mahon's conclusion.

In short, the crew had a map and a computer track that differed from each other, and nobody told them. Think about it: one coordinate changes in the dark of night, and a few hours later 257 people are flying along that route. The crew had been assured their path ran through the middle of McMurdo Sound. They had no idea the computer was taking them somewhere else.
So what was the sky like when Flight 901 neared Antarctica? And what sight fooled an entire crew? That is in the next part.

articleEn: As Flight 901 approached McMurdo Sound, a layer of cloud lay below. The crew decided to descend and take a look. The flight made a figure-eight manoeuvre and descended through a gap in the clouds over the water. The aim was to see ground features and give passengers a better view. The cloud base was later estimated at 600 to 900 metres.

What was the minimum safe altitude on the approved route? According to that route, the minimum safe altitude for approaching Erebus was 4,900 metres, and 1,800 metres in the southern sector, and that only in better weather. According to sources, the crew was either unaware of this limit or ignored it. But photographs and reports from earlier flights show that many flights had flown well below this minimum. In addition, briefings for earlier flights had said descent to any altitude was allowed with US ATC permission.

McMurdo's US controllers expected Flight 901 to come in over the Sound like earlier flights. They said their radar could track it down to 460 metres. But the radar never picked up the aircraft. VHF communication was also difficult, and the DME could not lock onto the TACAN for any useful period. Then Collins told McMurdo they were descending to 2,000 feet, or 600 metres. After that they put the aircraft on autopilot.

Now look at the scene outside. A layer of cloud had blended with the snow-covered volcano. There was no contrast between ground and sky. This is called sector whiteout. Everyone on the flight deck thought the white slope ahead was the Ross Ice Shelf, which was actually behind the mountain. Passenger photographs show that visibility was clear. Landmarks were visible 21 kilometres to the left and 16 kilometres to the right, under the clouds. So why wasn't the mountain seen?

According to sources, light was coming from directly behind the aircraft, filtering through the cloud layer. Shadows disappeared and Erebus vanished into the overcast sky. It was poorly understood, even by the company's experienced polar pilots. Air New Zealand had given the crew no training on sector whiteout.

The result was that the crew believed they were flying in McMurdo Sound. In reality they were over Lewis Bay, in front of Mount Erebus. It was now 12:49 pm. The ground proximity warning system, the GPWS, sounded. First came two whoops, then a command: "Pull up!" The cockpit voice recorder captured the Flight Engineer's voice: "500 feet," then "400 feet." The GPWS kept repeating "Pull up." The captain asked for go-around power, the command for a terrain escape manoeuvre. But it was far too late. Six seconds later, at 12:50 pm, the aircraft hit Mount Erebus. The impact was at 447 metres.
Now the question is: how did the world learn of it?

articleEn: After the crash, McMurdo Station tried to contact Flight 901 but failed. Airline headquarters in Auckland was told that contact had been lost. American search-and-rescue teams were put on standby. At 2:00 pm a US Navy situation report said Flight 901 had not responded to radio messages. An LC-130 aircraft and two UH-1N helicopters were preparing to depart. By 3:43 pm visibility was 64 kilometres and six aircraft had set out to search.

Meanwhile, at Christchurch airport, people were waiting for their loved ones. The flight was due at 6:05 pm, though some sources give 7:00 pm. Airport staff at first told families that a short delay was nothing unusual. But as time passed, it became clear something was wrong. At 9:00 pm, about half an hour after the time the fuel would have run out, Air New Zealand announced that it believed the aircraft was missing. Rescue teams searched along the expected route but found nothing.

Then at 12:55 am the crew of a US Navy aircraft saw wreckage on the slope of Mount Erebus. No survivors could be seen. At about 9:00 am, 20 hours after the crash, helicopters landed search parties on the mountain. They confirmed it was the wreckage of Flight 901. All 237 passengers and 20 crew had died. The aircraft's vertical stabiliser was found in the snow, with Air New Zealand's koru logo clearly visible.

Then Operation Overdue began, the mission to recover the dead from the crash site. It continued until 9 December 1979, with up to 60 personnel present at one time. One reason for the mission was pressure from Japan, since 24 passengers were Japanese. New Zealand Police officers and a mountain rescue team were flown out in a No. 40 Squadron C-130 Hercules. Inspector Jim Morgan led the mortuary team. Polar tents were set up at the site. Work went on for 24 hours a day in two shifts, 12 hours of work and 12 hours of rest. US Navy personnel were there too. Weather and skua gulls made the work very difficult. At one point, in bad weather, the team was even stranded on the mountain.

Identification took several weeks. Teams of pathologists, dentists and police kept records very carefully so the coroner could be satisfied. In the end, 83 percent of the passengers and crew were identified, sometimes by fingerprints and sometimes by small things such as keys in a pocket. Forty-four victims could not be identified individually. A funeral for all of them was held on 22 February 1980.

The service of those involved in Operation Overdue was later recognised. In 2006 the New Zealand Special Service Medal (Erebus) was created. It was also open to citizens of the United States and other countries, and a total of 40 Americans, mostly Navy personnel, are eligible.
So the wreckage was found, but the real question remained: who was responsible? Two different inquiries answered it, and their answers differed.

chapters.covers: Evidence: CVR, flight data recorder, passenger photographs ruling out a 'flying in cloud' theory; Chippindale's 12 June 1980 report blaming pilot error; public outcry; Justice Peter Mahon's Royal Commission, report 27 April 1981, clearing the crew and naming the waypoint change as the single dominant cause; sector whiteout and the 'malevolent trick of the polar light'; 'an orchestrated litany of lies'; judicial review, Court of Appeal, and the Privy Council ruling of 20 October 1983 that the conspiracy finding breached natural justice.

articleEn: First, let's look at the evidence. The cockpit voice recorder and the flight data recorder were both recovered in good condition, and their recordings could be understood. This was a sightseeing flight, so most passengers had cameras. A large part of the film from them could be developed. The photographs made one important point clear: in the pictures taken a few seconds before the crash, visibility was perfectly clear. Landmarks were visible on both sides below the cloud base, 21 kilometres to the left and 16 kilometres to the right. This ended the theory that the aircraft was flying in cloud.

On 12 June 1980 the report of New Zealand's chief inspector of air accidents, Ron Chippindale, was released. It named pilot error as the main cause. The blame fell on Captain Collins's decision to descend below the usual minimum altitude. According to the report, the crew was not entirely sure where the aircraft was, yet they continued at that altitude. But the public was not satisfied.

After strong public demand, the government announced another Royal Commission of Inquiry. It was a one-man commission led by Justice Peter Mahon. Its initial deadline was 31 October 1980, which was extended four times. Mahon's report came out on 27 April 1981. It cleared the crew of blame.

According to Mahon, the single, dominant and effective cause of the crash was that Air New Zealand changed the waypoint coordinates in the navigation computer and did not tell the crew. Mahon called the whiteout "a malevolent trick of the polar light." In his view, the crew could not visually recognise the mountain standing in front of them. He said they probably encountered sector whiteout, a rare phenomenon that creates the illusion of a distant flat horizon. According to Mahon, McMurdo's radio centre had cleared Collins to descend to 2,000 feet, which was below the 6,000-foot minimum.

Then came the most controversial part of the report. Mahon said that airline executives and senior pilots had conspired to whitewash the inquiry. He called it "an orchestrated litany of lies." That phrase echoed in New Zealand's popular culture for many years.

On 20 May 1981 Air New Zealand applied to the High Court for judicial review. The matter was referred to the Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal unanimously set aside Mahon's costs order, but the majority refused to overturn the conspiracy finding. Mahon appealed to the Privy Council in London. The decision came on 20 October 1983, and the appeal was dismissed. According to the judges, the conspiracy finding breached natural justice, and the evidence did not support it. The Privy Council accepted that the testimony of several executive pilots was wrong, but said it was not part of any pre-planned plan of deception.

Importantly, Mahon's conclusion about the crew stood: the crash was not pilot error, but the crew had been given wrong information about the route. So what changed after all this? And how do we remember the crash today?

articleEn: After Flight 901, Air New Zealand ended all its Antarctic flights. The last flight took place on 17 February 1980. Qantas also stopped its Antarctic flights in February 1980, and resumed them on a limited basis in 1994. Charter flights to Antarctica from New Zealand stayed suspended until 2013, when a Boeing 747-400 chartered from Qantas left Auckland for sightseeing.

The DC-10's reputation had already suffered. Six months earlier, American Airlines Flight 191 had crashed in Chicago. Air New Zealand's DC-10s were grounded for five weeks. From mid-1981 they were replaced with Boeing 747s, and the last DC-10 flew in December 1982.

Justice Mahon's report was presented to Parliament by Minister of Transport Maurice Williamson, long afterwards, in 1999. In 2009 Air New Zealand CEO Rob Fyfe apologised to all those who did not receive appropriate support and compassion from the company. On 28 November 2019, the 40th anniversary, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern apologised to the families on behalf of the airline, saying it had failed in its duty of care.

Memorials were also built. At Waikumete Cemetery in Auckland there is a memorial to the 44 victims, next to a cherry tree planted in memory of the 24 Japanese passengers. In January 2010 a sculpted 26 kg koru containing letters written by the victims' loved ones was placed near the Antarctic cross.

And the national memorial? In 2019 the Parnell Rose Gardens in Auckland were announced as the site, but local objections, an Ombudsman investigation and delays got in the way. Then, after the 2023 floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, land slips occurred, and engineers said the ground was not safe for a memorial. That plan came to an end. In November 2025 the Ministry named a new preferred site: Cracroft Reserve in Christchurch. Christchurch is the same city where the flight was to land first on its return.

Now for the lessons. The first is that one change in navigation data, if the crew is not told, can alter an aircraft's entire route. The second: every change must be communicated to the crew and the relevant controllers. In this case the telex carried only the word McMurdo instead of coordinates. The third lesson is about whiteout. The crew had received no training on sector whiteout, and even experienced polar pilots understood it poorly.
Some questions still seem open. The Privy Council held that several testimonies were wrong, but set aside the conspiracy finding. So how much of the whole truth came out?
Friends, on this day 257 people did not make it home. Their memory and the lessons of this crash should keep us alert. If you liked this video, please like it, share it and subscribe to the channel.

shorts.titleEn: Pull Up! The Final Seconds of Flight 901
shorts.text: ایک جہاز کے cockpit میں اچانک آواز گونجی: Pull up! یہ ground proximity warning system کا alarm تھا۔ 28 November 1979 کو Air New Zealand Flight 901 Antarctica کے اوپر تھی۔ پہلے دو whoop کی آوازیں آئیں، پھر مشین نے صاف کہا: Pull up! Flight engineer نے بتایا، 500 feet۔ پھر 400 feet۔ ہر لمحے زمین قریب آ رہی تھی۔ Captain نے کہا، go-around power please۔ یعنی engines کو پوری طاقت دو تاکہ جہاز اوپر اٹھ جائے۔ لیکن بہت دیر ہو چکی تھی۔ تقریباً 6 seconds بعد، دوپہر 12:50 پر، جہاز Mount Erebus سے ٹکرا گیا۔ اس پر 237 passengers اور 20 crew تھے۔ مگر crew کو اس پہاڑ کا اندازہ ہی کیوں نہیں ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek jahaz ke cockpit mein achanak awaz goonji: Pull up! Yeh ground proximity warning system ka alarm tha. 28 November 1979 ko Air New Zealand Flight 901 Antarctica ke upar thi. Pehle do whoop ki awazein aayein, phir machine ne saaf kaha: Pull up! Flight engineer ne bataya, 500 feet. Phir 400 feet. Har lamhe zameen qareeb aa rahi thi. Captain ne kaha, go-around power please. Yaani engines ko poori taqat do taake jahaz upar uth jaye. Lekin bohat der ho chuki thi. Taqriban 6 seconds baad, dopahar 12:50 par, jahaz Mount Erebus se takra gaya. Is par 237 passengers aur 20 crew thay. Magar crew ko is pahar ka andaza hi kyun nahin hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
The final seconds in the cockpit of Air New Zealand Flight 901 on 28 November 1979.
A respectful look at the warnings and the moments before impact on Mount Erebus.

shorts.titleEn: The Computer Change Nobody Told the Crew About
shorts.hook: Ek change, kisi ko pata nahin
shorts.text: ایک خاموش computer correction نے 257 لوگوں کی قسمت بدل دی! 14 November کو Captain Leslie Simpson نے ایک عجیب بات نوٹ کی۔ انہوں نے McMurdo کے TACAN beacon کے coordinates کا موازنہ اس waypoint سے کیا جو ان کے crew نے aircraft کے inertial navigation system میں ڈالا تھا۔ دونوں جگہوں کے درمیان فاصلہ بہت زیادہ تھا۔ Simpson نے Air New Zealand کے navigation section کو اس فرق کی اطلاع دی۔ اس کے بعد، حادثے والی صبح تقریباً 1:40 am پر، ground computer میں McMurdo waypoint کے coordinates بدل دیے گئے۔ مگر Flight 901 کے crew کو اس تبدیلی کے بارے میں بتایا ہی نہیں گیا۔ نئے coordinates کا مطلب کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek khamosh computer correction ne 257 logon ki qismat badal di! 14 November ko Captain Leslie Simpson ne ek ajeeb baat note ki. Unhon ne McMurdo ke TACAN beacon ke coordinates ka muwazna us waypoint se kiya jo un ke crew ne aircraft ke inertial navigation system mein dala tha. Dono jaghon ke darmiyan fasla bohat zyada tha. Simpson ne Air New Zealand ke navigation section ko is farq ki ittila di. Is ke baad, hadsay wali subah taqriban 1:40 am par, ground computer mein McMurdo waypoint ke coordinates badal diye gaye. Magar Flight 901 ke crew ko is tabdeeli ke bare mein bataya hi nahin gaya. Naye coordinates ka matlab kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
How a navigation coordinate change made hours before departure went unnoticed by the Flight 901 crew.
The story starts with Captain Leslie Simpson's observation on 14 November 1979.

shorts.titleEn: The Photos That Ended the 'Flying in Cloud' Theory
shorts.text: ایک جہاز کے passengers کی تصویروں نے کیسے ایک theory کو ختم کر دیا؟ Flight 901 ایک sightseeing flight تھی، اس لیے زیادہ تر passengers کے پاس cameras تھے۔ حادثے سے چند seconds پہلے کی photographs میں visibility بالکل صاف تھی۔ Cloud base کے نیچے دونوں طرف landmarks نظر آ رہے تھے، 21 kilometres بائیں اور 16 kilometres دائیں۔ یوں flying in cloud والی theory ختم ہو گئی۔ پھر 12 June 1980 کو chief inspector Ron Chippindale کی report جاری ہوئی، جس نے pilot error کو بنیادی وجہ قرار دیا۔ لیکن public نے جواب مانگا، اور Justice Peter Mahon کا Royal Commission بنا۔ اس کا نتیجہ پہلی report سے بالکل مختلف تھا۔ وہ کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek jahaz ke passengers ki tasveeron ne kaise ek theory ko khatam kar diya? Flight 901 ek sightseeing flight thi, is liye zyada tar passengers ke paas cameras thay. Hadsay se chand seconds pehle ki photographs mein visibility bilkul saaf thi. Cloud base ke neeche dono taraf landmarks nazar aa rahe thay, 21 kilometres bayen aur 16 kilometres dayen. Yun flying in cloud wali theory khatam ho gayi. Phir 12 June 1980 ko chief inspector Ron Chippindale ki report jari hui, jis ne pilot error ko bunyadi wajah qarar diya. Lekin public ne jawab manga, aur Justice Peter Mahon ka Royal Commission bana. Is ka nateeja pehli report se bilkul mukhtalif tha. Woh kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Passenger photographs showed clear visibility just before the Flight 901 crash and ruled out a cloud theory.
Two inquiries, the Chippindale report and the Mahon Royal Commission, reached very different conclusions.
